**Surah al-Nasr**

It is also called "Surah Idha Ja'a" (When it comes). It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that it is called "Surah al-Taw'if" (the Surah of Farewell), because it contains an allusion to the death of the Prophet, upon him be peace, and his bidding farewell to this world and what is in it.

It is reported in several narrations from Ibn 'Abbas and others that when it was revealed, he (ﷺ) said: "My death has been announced to me" (*nu'iyat ilayya nafsi*).

In a narration of al-Bayhaqi from him, when it was revealed, upon him be peace, he summoned Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, and said: "Indeed my death has been announced to me." She wept, then laughed. She was asked about it, and she said: "He told me that his death had been announced to him, so I wept. Then he told me that you would be the first of my family to join me, so I laughed."

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, understood this from it, and after this the Prophet, upon him be peace, would act like one bidding farewell.

It is Madani (revealed in Madinah) according to the more correct view in the definition of the Madani (the Surah revealed after the Hijrah), for al-Tirmidhi in his *Musnad* and al-Bayhaqi narrated from the hadith of Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, 'Abdullah ibn Dinar and Sadaqah ibn Bashshar, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "This Surah was revealed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, in the middle of the days of Tashriq at Mina, while he was in the Farewell Pilgrimage: ﴿When the help of Allah and the victory come﴾, until he completed it..." The report continues.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and others also narrated it, but the Hafiz Ibn Rajab said after citing it from the first two: "Its chain of narration is very weak. Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, Ahmad said: narrating from him is not permitted." If it is authentic, then its revelation was very close to the time of the death of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, for the period between the Farewell Pilgrimage and his answering the call of the True Lord (upon him be peace) was three months and a little more.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah that he said: "By Allah, the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, did not live after the revelation of ﴿When the help of Allah and the victory come﴾ for long, two years, then he passed away, upon him be peace."

In *al-Bahr* (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit): its revelation was when he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, returned from Khaybar. You know that the Battle of Khaybar took place in the seventh year, at the end of Muharram, so the interval would be more than two years. Its being Madani is also indicated by what Muslim, Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "The last Surah revealed in the Qur'an in its entirety is: ﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾." Its number of verses is three by consensus. In it is an indication of the fading away of the religion of idols and the manifestation of the religion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in its most complete form, and this is the aspect of its connection (*munasabah*) with what precedes it. Other things are possible. It is, according to what al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from the hadith of Anas, that ﴿When the help of Allah and the victory come﴾ is a quarter of the Qur'an.

I have not found the reason for this, and what relates to it will come, if Allah Most High wills.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾: that is, His Most High assistance and His making you prevail over your enemy. This is the meaning of *nasr* (help) when it is followed by *'ala* (over), and it is interpreted accordingly because it is more suitable with His saying, Most High: ﴿and the victory﴾. It is also permitted that it be meant with the construction followed by *min* (from), and its meaning would be protection. And *al-fath* (the victory) includes *al-nasr* in the first sense. Then the speech would contain the benefit of both kinds of help. The first is the apparent meaning.

*Idha* (when) is in the accusative, governed by *sabbih* (glorify). The *fa'* (fa) does not prevent this, according to what the majority hold regarding such cases. Abu Hayyan holds that it is governed by the verb after it and is not a noun in construct with it. Another view will come, if Allah Most High wills. The intended help here is what occurred in the affair of Makkah, of his, upon him be peace, prevailing over Quraysh. Al-Naqqash mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that the help is the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which took place at the end of the sixth year. As for the victory, a group narrated from him and from 'A'ishah that it refers to the Conquest of Makkah. This was narrated from Mujahid and others, and the majority declared it sound. It took place in the eighth year. Ibn Shihab said: on the thirteenth night remaining of the month of Ramadan, at the head of eight years and a half after the Hijrah.

He, upon him be peace, set out, according to what Ahmad narrated with a sound chain from Abu Sa'id, two nights past the month of Ramadan. In another narration from Ahmad, it was on the eighteenth; in another, on the twelfth; and in Muslim's, on the sixteenth. Al-Waqidi said: the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, set out on Wednesday, ten nights past Ramadan, after the 'Asr prayer. Al-Qastallani declared this weak. The Muslims in that campaign were ten thousand, from the Muhajirun and the Ansar and groups from the Arabs. In *al-Iklil*: twelve thousand.

*Page 256*

It is reconciled by saying that he, upon him be peace, set out from Madinah with ten thousand, then two thousand joined them later. The better view is that the help is to be understood as what occurred together with the aforementioned Conquest. If the noble Surah was revealed before that, then the matter is clear, and it includes the announcement of that before it occurred, which is among the signs of prophethood. If it was revealed after it, then al-Maturidi said in *al-Ta'wilat*: *idha* here has the meaning of *idh*, which is for the past, and its use with this meaning is frequent in the Qur'an. In that case it is connected to an implied element, such as "He completed the matter," or "He perfected the blessing upon the servants," or something similar, and not to "glorify." Because the speech in that case would be like: "I struck Zayd yesterday." Some eminent scholars said: it is for the future, as is most common in its usage. In that case it is necessary to make some part of it future and continuing, on the basis that the Conquest of Makkah was the mother of conquests and the foundation for what would come after it. So it is awaited in terms of what it indicates, even if it is established in itself in terms of its own reality. It is also permitted that the futurity be considered in terms of the whole of what lies within the scope of *idha*, of which part is future, and that is what it includes...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 110, verse 2:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you see the people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes﴾. It may also be taken in another sense, which is included, and there is no harm in this so long as the descent (nuzul) does not come after the completion of the entry. It has been said that what is meant is the category of Allah the Exalted's help to His Messenger (ﷺ) and to the believers, and the category of the conquest (fath). This includes what occurred concerning Makkah, may Allah increase its honour, and other matters. The matter of the qibla is clear in this regard. In any case, what is meant by "coming" (al-maji') is "attainment" (al-husul), and it is literally used in this sense, as the apparent meaning of al-Raghib's words requires. al-Qadi said: it is figurative (majaz). The apparent meaning is that the address in "you see" (ra'ayta) is to the Prophet (ﷺ). The seeing is either visual (basariyyah) or cognitive ('ilmiyyah), transitive to two objects. "The people" (al-nas) refers to the Arabs. "The religion of Allah" (din Allah) is the community of Islam (millat al-Islam), and there is no other religion that Allah the Exalted may be attributed to. Al-afwaj is the plural of fawj, which, according to al-Raghib, is "a passing, hurrying group," and it is used to mean any group in general. al-Hufi said: the analogical plural of it would be afwuj, but the damma was felt to be heavy upon the waw, so it was changed to afwaj. In al-Bahr: the analogical plural of a triliteral form with a sound middle radical (fi'l) is af'ul, not af'al, while one with a weak middle radical is the reverse, so the analogical form for it is af'al, like hawd and ahwad. The form af'ul was used irregularly for it, as in thawb and athwub.

The accusative of (afwajan) is a circumstantial (hal) construction from the pronoun in (yadkhulun). As for the clause (yadkhulun), it is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing "the people" on the first possibility regarding the seeing, and a second object (maf'ul thani) on the second possibility. It may also be a circumstantial clause if ra'ayta is taken to mean 'arafta (you knew), as al-Zamakhshari said. Abu Hayyan objected to this by saying: "We do not know that ra'ayta comes with the meaning of 'arafta, so this requires verification." What is meant by the people's entry into His religion in multitudes is large groups, whose Islam came without fighting. This occurred between the conquest of Makkah and the Messenger's death (ﷺ). Before the conquest, they used to enter it one by one or two by two.

al-Bukhari transmitted from Amr ibn Salama, who said: "When the conquest came, every people hastened to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with their Islam. The tribes had been waiting to see about their Islam, [the outcome of] the conquest of Makkah, and they would say: 'Leave him and his people; if he prevails over them, then he is a prophet.'"

And from al-Hasan, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, the Bedouins said: 'Now that he has triumphed over the people of Makkah, whom Allah protected from the People of the Elephant, you have no power against him.' So they entered the religion of Allah in multitudes."

Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die while there remained a single unbelieving man among the Arabs. Rather, all entered Islam after Hunayn and al-Ta'if; some came in person, and some sent delegations." Ibn Atiyya interpreted this and said: "The meaning, and Allah knows best, is the Arabs who worshipped idols. The Christians of Banu Taghlib, I do not think, accepted Islam during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they paid the jizya (poll tax). Some have explicitly stated that they did not accept Islam at that time. Therefore, the people (al-nas) means the idolatrous Arabs, such as the people of Makkah, al-Ta'if, Yemen, Hawazin, and others like them."

Ikrimah and Muqatil said: "The people (al-nas) means the people of Yemen, from whom seven hundred men came as a delegation and accepted Islam." They cited in support what Ibn Jarir transmitted through the chain of al-Husayn ibn Isa, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Hazim, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Madinah, he said: 'Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, the help of Allah and the victory have come, and the people of Yemen have come.' It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who are the people of Yemen?' He said: 'A people whose hearts are tender and soft; their obedience is faith. Understanding (al-fiqh) is Yamani, and wisdom is Yamani.'"

He also transmitted it through the chain of Abd al-A'la, from Ma'mar, from Ikrimah, as a mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain).

As for his saying (ﷺ), "Faith is Yamani" (al-iman yamani), it appears in a hadith transmitted by al-Bukhari, Muslim, and al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayra, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), in the wording: "The people of Yemen have come to you; they are more tender of heart and softer of hearts. Faith is Yamani, and wisdom is Yamani." It has been said: he (ﷺ) said this because Makkah is Yamani, and from it he was sent (ﷺ), and faith spread. It has also been said: he (ﷺ) intended to praise the Ansar, for they are Yamani, and they settled in the abode and faith. Ibn Abbas's statement in the report, "in Madinah," contradicts the view of those who say that he (ﷺ) said this at Tabuk. Between him and Yemen lie Makkah and Madinah, which are the two abodes of faith and its places of manifestation. It is possible that the statement was repeated. The apparent meaning is that it is praise of the people of Yemen for their haste to faith and their acceptance of it without a sword. It includes the Ansar and others from Yemen. It is as though faith was in the very essence of their hearts, so they accepted it as it was presented to them, like one who finds what he has lost. Similar to this in praising them is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "I find the breath of your Lord coming from the direction of Yemen."

Isam al-Din said: "It is possible that the address in 'you see the people' is general to every believer." Then he said: "What occurs to the heart is that what suits Allah the Exalted's words, ﴿they enter the religion of Allah in multitudes﴾, is that His words, glorified is He, ﴿and the victory﴾ should be taken as the opening of the door of religion to them." End of quotation.

Both of these matters are as you see. Ibn Abbas recited, as Abu Ubayda and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him: "When there comes the victory of Allah and the help." Ibn Kathir, in one narration, recited "yudkhalun" in the passive voice.

﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾: that is, declare Him exalted, with every expression that indicates His transcendence (tanzih), praising Him, may He be majestic and exalted, in addition to worship of Him and extolling Him, may He be glorified, for the increase of His bounties upon you. So tasbih (glorification) is tanzih (declaring God free of imperfection), not merely uttering the phrase subhan Allah. The ba' is for accompaniment (mulabasah), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The noun hamd is in the genitive construction with the object. The meaning is a combination of glorifying Him, exalted is He, which is declaring Him free of whatever is unbefitting of Him, mighty and majestic, of deficiencies, and praising Him, which is affirming what befits Him of praiseworthy attributes, because of the greatness of what He, glorified is He, has bestowed upon him, peace and blessings be upon him.

It was also said: that is, declare Him exalted above weakness in delaying the manifestation of the conquest, and praise Him for the delay, describing Him, exalted is He, as one whose timing of affairs is from Him and is only for a wisdom that none knows but Him, mighty and majestic. This is as you see, and it is supported by what is in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) from Masruq, from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to frequently say in his bowing and prostration: 'Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me.'"

He is interpreting the Qur'an; you mean this together with His saying, ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾, that is, ask Him to forgive you. Likewise with what is in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad and Sahih Muslim, also from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to frequently say near the end of his life: 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, I seek Allah's forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance (tawba).'" And he said: "My Lord informed me that I would see a sign among my nation, and commanded me that when I see it I should glorify Him with His praise and seek His forgiveness." Etc.

Ibn Jarir narrated through the chain of Hafs ibn Asim, from al-Sha'bi, from Umm Salamah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, near the end of his life, would not stand, sit, go, or come without saying: 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him.' He said: 'I have been commanded with it,' and then recited the surah." This report is gharib (weak or singular).

In the Musnad, from Abu Ubaydah, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When ﴿When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest﴾ was revealed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, he used to frequently say, when he recited it and bowed: 'Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me, indeed You are the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful,' three times."

It is also permissible that the ba' is for seeking help (isti'anah), and the hamd is in the genitive construction with the subject; meaning, glorified is He with what He has praised Himself with. Ibn Rajab said: since not every glorification is praiseworthy, the glorification of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) entails negating many attributes. Bishr al-Marisi used to say: "Glory be to my Lord the Lowest," exalted is Allah above that, greatly exalted. The apparent meaning is accompaniment. It is also permissible that tasbih is a metaphor for wonder (ta'ajjub), by the relation of causation: for whoever sees a wondrous matter says "Glory be to Allah," meaning: so marvel at Allah's facilitation of what did not occur to you or anyone's mind, that anyone would overcome the people of the Sacred Precinct (Haram). And praise Him, exalted is He, for His doing. This wonder is the wonder of one who reflects and is grateful, and it is correct to be commanded with it. The command is not in the sense of a report, on the basis that this story is something one should marvel at, as Ibn al-Munayyir claimed. The justification that the command in the form of wonder is not a clearly invalid command is also not decisive. Indeed, this view is nothing, and the reports indicate that this is a command to him, peace and blessings be upon him, to prepare to turn toward his Lord, exalted is He, and to prepare to meet Him after he had perfected his religion and fulfilled what was upon him of conveying the message. Also, what we have mentioned of the narrations just above does not support it.

It was said: the intended meaning of tasbih is prayer, because it includes it, and Ibn al-Jawzi narrated this from Ibn Abbas; that is: pray to Him, exalted is He, praising Him for His bounties. It has been reported that when he entered Makkah, peace and blessings be upon him, he prayed in the house of Umm Hani eight rak'ahs. Some claimed that he prayed them inside the Ka'bah, but this is not correct.

In any case, it is the Prayer of Conquest (salat al-fath), and it is a recommended practice (sunnah). Sa'd prayed it on the day of the conquest of al-Mada'in. It was also said it is the Duha prayer, and it was said four of them are for the conquest and four for the Duha. In any case there is no evidence in it that the intended meaning of tasbih is prayer, and the reports also support a different understanding. And his seeking forgiveness, peace and blessings be upon him, it was said, is because he was always ascending, so when he reached a station he sought forgiveness for what came before it. It was also said: for what is, in his noble view, contrary to what is better for his lofty rank. It was also said: for whatever lapse occurred, even if it is said this refers to prophethood. It was said it is to teach his nation, peace and blessings be upon him. It was also said: it is a seeking of forgiveness for his nation, peace and blessings be upon him; that is: and seek His forgiveness for your nation. Some permitted that the address in "you saw" is general, and said: here it is permissible then that the command to seek forgiveness is for others besides him, peace and blessings be upon him, and his inclusion in the command is by way of prevailing (taghlib). This is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning. You know that everyone falls short in fulfilling the rights of Allah, exalted is He, as they should be, and in rendering them in the manner befitting His majesty, may His majesty and greatness be glorified. Each person renders them according to what he knows, and the one who knows Allah knows that the measure of Allah, mighty and majestic, is higher and greater than that. So he feels shame for his deed and sees himself as falling short. The more a person knows Allah, the more fearful of Him he becomes, and by seeing his shortcoming he becomes more perceptive. Kahmas used to pray a thousand rak'ahs every day, and when he finished prayer he would take hold of his beard and then say to himself: "Stand up, O refuge of every evil! By Allah, I have not been pleased with you for Allah, mighty and majestic, for the blink of an eye." And from Malik ibn Dinar: "I have really considered that when I die, I should be instructed that I be taken away as a runaway slave is taken to his master, and when He asks me, I will say: 'O Lord, I have not been pleased with myself for You for the blink of an eye.'" So it is possible that his seeking forgiveness, peace and blessings be upon him, is for what he knows of the great majesty of Allah, exalted is He, and His greatness, glorified is He, so he sees that his worship, though it is the most sublime of the worship of all worshippers, falls short of what befits that majesty and that greatness, which lie beyond what occurs to the mind. So he feels shame and hastens to seek forgiveness.

It has been authentically reported that "he, peace be upon him, used to seek Allah's forgiveness in a day and a night more than seventy times." And to indicate the shortcoming of the worshipper in bringing what befits the majesty of the One worshipped, and that exerting effort is insufficient, seeking forgiveness has been prescribed after many acts of worship. They mentioned that it is prescribed for one who prays the obligatory prayer to seek forgiveness three times after it, and for the one who prays at night in the last part of the night to seek forgiveness as much as Allah wills, and for the pilgrim to seek forgiveness after Hajj. For Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness of Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

It was reported that it is prescribed at the completion of wudu' (ablution). They said: it is prescribed at the end of every gathering.

And "he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say when he rose from a gathering: 'Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance.'"

So in the command to seek forgiveness there is a hint, in this respect, according to what has been said, toward what was understood of the announcement of his death. The well-known view is that it indicates the approach of the completion of the matter of the call and the perfection of the religion. And although the statement includes a conditional form and the placing of glorification before praise and then seeking forgiveness, it was said: it follows the manner of descent from the Creator to the creation, as it is said: "I have not seen anything except that I saw Allah, exalted is He, before it," because all things are mirrors for His manifestation, majestic is His majesty. That is because in glorification and praise there is a turning toward the essence of the majesty and perfection of the Creator, and in seeking forgiveness there is a turning toward the state of the servant and his shortcomings. It is also possible that seeking forgiveness is placed after them for what we pointed out regarding the prescription of following worship with seeking forgiveness. It was also said that placing glorification before it teaches the etiquette of supplication, which is not to ask abruptly without first praising the One being asked.

﴿Indeed He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾: that is, from the time He created the accountable beings; that is, exceedingly accepting of their repentance. So the one seeking forgiveness, who repents, should expect acceptance. The clause is in the position of giving a reason for what precedes it. The choice of "Accepting of repentance" (tawwab) over "Forgiving" (ghaffar), although the latter is what "seek His forgiveness" apparently requires, is for alerting, as some of the eminent scholars said, that seeking forgiveness only benefits when it is accompanied by repentance.

Ibn Rajab mentioned that bare istighfar (seeking forgiveness) is repentance together with asking for forgiveness through supplication, and the combined form, "I seek Allah's forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance," is asking for forgiveness through supplication only. He also said: bare istighfar is asking for protection from the evil of a past sin through supplication and regret over it, and protection from the evil of an expected sin through resolve to abandon it. This is what prevents persistence (israr), as it has come: "One who seeks forgiveness does not persist in sin even if he returns to it seventy times in a day, and there is no minor sin with persistence, and no major sin with seeking forgiveness."

The combined form with repentance is specific to the first type; if it is not accompanied by regret over the past sin, it is pure supplication, and if it is accompanied by regret, it is repentance. End of quote.

The apparent view is that this pure supplication is not accepted, and in it is much bad etiquette with Allah, exalted is He. Some eminent scholars said: in this verse there is ihtibak (a rhetorical device of omission from each of two parts of what the other supplies), and the original is: "and seek His forgiveness, indeed He is ever Forgiving, and turn to Him, indeed He is ever Accepting of repentance." This is supported by what we mentioned earlier from the hadith of Imam Ahmad and Muslim from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. Taking the past tense as referring to the time of the creation of the accountable beings is what many have approved. Al-Maturidi said in al-Ta'wilat: that is, He has never ceased to be Accepting of repentance, not that He, exalted is He, became Accepting of repentance by an attribute He acquired and produced, according to what the Mu'tazilah say, that He, exalted is He, became Accepting of repentance when He brought creation into being and they repented, and He accepted their repentance, whereas before that He was not Accepting of repentance. It was refuted that the acceptance of repentance is among the relational attributes (sifat idafiyyah), and there is no dispute about their being originated. Some preferred what al-Maturidi held, that the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, has always been such that He accepts repentance, and its consequence is the eternity of the source of accepting it from the attributes befitting Him, glorified is His majesty. In this there is something that strengthens hope in Him, mighty and majestic, to a degree.

It is authentically reported: "Had you not sinned, Allah would have taken you away and brought a people who sin and then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them. And in seeking forgiveness is the good of this world and the Hereafter."

Imam Ahmad narrated from the hadith of Atiyyah, from Abu Sa'id, raised (marfu'): "Whoever says when he goes to his bed: 'I seek the forgiveness of Allah, other than whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and I turn to Him in repentance,' his sins will be forgiven even if they are like the foam of the sea, and even if they are like the sand of 'Aalij, and even if they are like the number of the leaves of trees."

He also narrated from the hadith of Ibn Abbas: "Whoever frequently seeks forgiveness, Allah, exalted is He, will grant him relief from every distress."

And I say: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him. I seek Allah's forgiveness, exalted is He, and turn to Him in repentance, and I ask Him to grant me relief from every distress and a way out from every narrowness, by the sanctity of His Book and by the master of His beloved ones, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him.
